Editor's note: Dan Buettner is the best-selling author of "The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who've Lived the Longest."   Watch Buettner's reports from Greece all week on "AC360°" Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis, 73,  lives in Ikaria nearly 40 years after a diagnosis of stomach cancer. Ikaria, GREECE (CNN) -- In 1970, when doctors diagnosed Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis with stomach cancer and only gave him a few months to live, he decided to move back to Ikaria, his birth island. There, he reasoned, he could be buried more inexpensively among his fellow Greeks.   But when he moved back to the island he didn't die. He has lived nearly 40 years more. And when he returned to America on a recent visit, he discovered that his doctors were all dead. The people on this 99-square-mile Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea smugly tell this story as yet another example of what they've always known and scientists are now discovering: People in Ikaria live longer than in just about any other place in the world. A recent study of 90-year-old siblings, conducted by the National Hellenic Research Foundation, discovered 10 times more 90-year-old brothers and sisters here than the European average. Why is this important? Most scientists agree that the average human should live to age 90. (You have to have won the genetic lottery to live to 100.) But the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says life expectancy in America is 78. Somewhere along the line, we're losing about a dozen years -- most of them to costly and potentially preventable chronic diseases such as heart attacks, diabetes and cancer. These diseases are dragging down our health care system and account for much of the reason why the National Institute on Aging says the average American suffers about three disabled end-of-life years during which they incur 90 percent of our lifelong health care costs.   Ikarians are avoiding these diseases and reaching age 90 at a rate of about four times the rate that Americans do. They are getting the good years we're missing, dying quickly and less expensively. For the next two weeks, I'm leading "The Blue Zones" expedition, an AARP and National Geographic sponsored team of the world's best demographers, physicians, medical researchers and media specialists, to explore Ikarian longevity. We already have a few clues. Since at least the sixth century B.C., Icaria was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans as a health destination -- largely for its hot springs believed to relieve pain, joint problems and skin ailments. Our team has reviewed reports of high levels of radon in these baths and will be exploring a theory that chronic exposure to low-level radiation may help protect DNA against the ravages of aging. For much of the ensuing two millenniums, people here lived in relative isolation. The people here evolved a unique diet that we believe is a more heart-protective version of the Mediterranean diet. We're doing pharmacological analyses of dozens of herbal teas and unique honey produced by bees that draw pollen of thyme, fir and erica. We think we'll find anti-cancer, anti-oxidant and probiotic properties in these locally produced products. We also know that people here have a vastly different character than the rest of the Mediterranean. They have volcanic tempers that quickly subside. Despite living on harsh, steep terrain, they're known for relentless optimism and three-day parties. They don't get stressed by deadlines. They go to bed well after midnight, sleep late and take naps. Anecdotally, we know that most people over 90 are sexually active. Do these people possess the true secret to longevity? We're not sure yet, but we'll certainly distill a few clues about living longer, better. Ikarian wisdom may not help you live to 100. But at least they may help you outlive your doctor. Follow and vote to direct Dan's expedition at aarp.org/bluezones . The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Dan Buettner.

**Editor’s note:** Dan Buettner is the best-selling author of *The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who’ve Lived the Longest.* Watch Buettner’s reports from Greece all week on *AC360°*.

Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis, 73, has lived in Ikaria for nearly 40 years following a diagnosis of stomach cancer.

**IKARIA, Greece (CNN) —** In 1970, when doctors diagnosed Greek-American Yiannis Karimalis with stomach cancer and gave him only a few months to live, he decided to return to Ikaria, the island of his birth. There, he reasoned, he could be buried less expensively among his fellow Greeks.

But after returning to the island, he did not die. He has lived for nearly 40 more years. And when he recently visited America, he discovered that all his doctors had died.

The people of this 99-square-mile Greek island in the eastern Aegean Sea recount this story with some satisfaction, regarding it as yet another example of what they have always known—and what scientists are now discovering: People in Ikaria live longer than those in nearly any other place in the world.

A recent study of 90-year-old siblings, conducted by the National Hellenic Research Foundation, found 10 times as many 90-year-old brothers and sisters here as the European average.

Why is this important? Most scientists agree that the average human should live to age 90. Living to 100, however, requires winning the genetic lottery. Yet according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, life expectancy in America is 78. Somewhere along the way, we are losing about a dozen years—most of them to costly and potentially preventable chronic diseases such as heart attacks, diabetes and cancer.

These diseases are straining our health care system and account for much of the reason the National Institute on Aging says the average American experiences about three years of disability at the end of life, during which 90 percent of lifetime health care costs are incurred.

Ikarians are avoiding these diseases and reaching age 90 at about four times the rate of Americans. They are enjoying the healthy years we are missing, then dying quickly and less expensively.

For the next two weeks, I am leading “The Blue Zones” expedition—an AARP- and National Geographic-sponsored team of the world’s leading demographers, physicians, medical researchers and media specialists—to investigate Ikarian longevity.

We already have a few clues. Since at least the sixth century B.C., Ikaria was known to the ancient Greeks and Romans as a health destination, largely because of its hot springs, which were believed to relieve pain, joint problems and skin ailments. Our team has reviewed reports of high radon levels in these baths and will explore the theory that chronic exposure to low-level radiation may help protect DNA from the ravages of aging.

For much of the following two millennia, people here lived in relative isolation. They developed a distinctive diet that we believe is a more heart-protective version of the Mediterranean diet.

We are conducting pharmacological analyses of dozens of herbal teas, as well as unique honey produced by bees that gather pollen from thyme, fir and erica. We believe these locally produced foods may have anti-cancer, antioxidant and probiotic properties.

We also know that the people here have a character markedly different from that found elsewhere in the Mediterranean. They have volcanic tempers that quickly subside. Despite living amid harsh, steep terrain, they are known for their relentless optimism and three-day parties.

They do not become stressed by deadlines. They go to bed well after midnight, sleep late and take naps. Anecdotally, we know that most people over 90 remain sexually active.

Do these people possess the true secret to longevity? We are not yet sure, but we will certainly distill a few insights into living longer and better.

Ikarian wisdom may not help you live to 100. But it may at least help you outlive your doctor.

Follow Dan’s expedition and vote to help direct it at **aarp.org/bluezones**.

*The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of Dan Buettner.*

**Editor’s note:** Dan Buettner wrote the best-selling book *“The Blue Zones: Lessons for Living Longer from the People Who’ve Lived the Longest.”* His reports from Greece will air throughout the week on *“AC360°.”*

**IKARIA, Greece (CNN)** — Yiannis Karimalis, a 73-year-old Greek-American, has lived on Ikaria for almost four decades beyond the time doctors expected him to survive stomach cancer.

After receiving the diagnosis in 1970 and being told that he had only a few months left, Karimalis returned to the Greek island where he was born. He believed that being buried among other Greeks there would cost less.

Instead of dying, however, he survived for nearly another 40 years. During a recent trip back to the United States, he learned that all the physicians who had treated him had already died.

Residents of Ikaria—a 99-square-mile island in the eastern Aegean Sea—recount his experience with some satisfaction. To them, it confirms something they have long believed and researchers are now beginning to recognize: Ikarians enjoy exceptional longevity compared with people in almost every other part of the world.

A recent National Hellenic Research Foundation study examining siblings in their 90s found that Ikaria had 10 times as many brothers and sisters of that age as the European average.

Why does that matter? Most researchers believe the typical person should be capable of reaching 90, while surviving to 100 generally requires extraordinary genetic luck. Yet the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports that U.S. life expectancy is 78. Americans are therefore losing roughly 12 potential years, largely because of expensive chronic illnesses that may be preventable, including cancer, diabetes and heart attacks.

These conditions place a heavy burden on the health care system. According to the National Institute on Aging, the average American spends approximately the final three years of life with a disability, and that period generates 90 percent of the person’s lifetime health care expenses.

Ikarians largely escape these illnesses and reach 90 at about four times the American rate. In other words, they experience the healthy years many Americans miss, then tend to die more rapidly and at lower cost.

Over the next two weeks, I will lead *The Blue Zones* expedition, supported by AARP and National Geographic. The group brings together leading demographers, doctors, medical scientists and media professionals to investigate why Ikarians live so long.

Some possible explanations have already emerged. As far back as the sixth century B.C., ancient Greeks and Romans regarded Icaria as a place of healing, mainly because its hot springs were thought to ease pain, skin disorders and joint difficulties.

Our researchers have examined findings showing elevated radon concentrations in the baths. We will investigate the possibility that long-term exposure to small amounts of radiation could help shield DNA from age-related damage.

For much of the following 2,000 years, the island’s population remained comparatively isolated. Over that time, residents developed a distinctive way of eating that we suspect may protect the heart even more effectively than the standard Mediterranean diet.

We are also conducting pharmacological tests on dozens of local herbal infusions, along with an unusual honey made by bees gathering pollen from erica, fir and thyme. We believe these island products may contain probiotic, antioxidant and cancer-fighting qualities.

Ikarians also have a temperament unlike that found elsewhere in the Mediterranean. Their anger can erupt dramatically but disappears just as fast. Although they inhabit rugged, sharply sloping land, they are famous for tireless optimism and celebrations that continue for three days.

Deadlines cause them little anxiety. They stay awake well past midnight, rise late and nap during the day. Informal accounts also indicate that most islanders older than 90 remain sexually active.

Have they uncovered the real formula for a long life? We cannot say yet, but we expect to identify at least several lessons for living both longer and more fully.

Following Ikarian practices may not carry you to 100, but they might at least enable you to live longer than your physician.

You can follow Dan’s journey and vote on the expedition’s direction at **aarp.org/bluezones**.

The views presented in this commentary belong exclusively to Dan Buettner.

### Ikaria’s longevity lesson: A long life is built into the day

On the Greek island of Ikaria, longevity is not treated as a project. There are no elaborate wellness regimens, age-defying products or rigid schedules. Instead, many residents simply live in a way that makes healthy choices almost unavoidable.

That is what made Ikaria so compelling to the Blue Zones expedition investigating communities where people live unusually long lives. Researchers found not a single miracle food or genetic secret, but a web of mutually reinforcing habits.

Ikarians tend to eat a traditional Mediterranean-style diet rich in vegetables, beans, whole grains, olive oil and wild greens. They move naturally by tending gardens, walking through steep villages and doing household tasks. Afternoon naps are common. Religious fasting periodically limits calories and animal products. Strong family ties and frequent social contact help keep older people connected to community life.

Even the island’s relaxed relationship with time may matter. Social gatherings can last for hours, and the day is not always governed by the clock. Chronic stress is difficult to measure, but its effects on cardiovascular and metabolic health are well established. Ikaria suggests that a culture designed around companionship, rest and purpose may help soften that burden.

None of this proves that copying one Ikarian custom will add years to anyone’s life. Longevity reflects genetics, environment, health care, chance and behavior. Nor should the island be romanticized; it faces the same pressures of modernization and population change as many rural communities.

The larger lesson is more practical. Most people do not need more information about healthy living. They need surroundings that make healthy living easier.

Ikaria’s real achievement may be that movement, nutritious food, social connection and a sense of belonging are woven into ordinary life. Its oldest residents remind us that longevity is rarely created by one dramatic decision. More often, it is the cumulative result of thousands of small choices—many of them shaped by the places and people around us.

# The island where a terminal diagnosis was not the end

When Yiannis Karimalis was diagnosed with terminal stomach cancer, the prognosis left little room for hope. Yet he returned to Ikaria, his Greek island home, resumed the rhythms of village life—and survived far beyond the time doctors had expected.

His story is extraordinary, but on Ikaria, longevity itself is not. The mountainous island in the eastern Aegean has become famous for its unusually large population of people who remain active into their 80s and 90s. Researchers have counted it among the world’s so-called “Blue Zones,” places where reaching old age appears more common than in industrialized countries such as the United States.

No one can say that Ikaria cured Karimalis. Individual cancer outcomes can defy forecasts, diagnoses and prognoses are not infallible, and anecdotes are not clinical evidence. But his survival reflects the question that has drawn doctors and demographers to the island: Why do so many Ikarians seem to live longer—and often healthier—than Americans?

The answer is probably not one miracle food or a hidden longevity gene. It is a way of life assembled from many small protections.

## Movement without exercise plans

Ikarians rarely describe themselves as fitness enthusiasts. Traditionally, they have not needed to. Villages are built on steep slopes; homes, gardens, churches and neighbors are often reached on foot. Older residents tend vines, prune olive trees, keep animals and work vegetable plots.

That routine creates frequent, low-intensity movement of the kind modern Americans are often advised to add back into sedentary days. It can help preserve muscle, balance and cardiovascular health without requiring a gym membership.

In the United States, by contrast, daily life is frequently organized around cars, desks, elevators and screens. Exercise may be intense but confined to a few scheduled sessions, while much of the rest of the day is spent sitting.

## A diet shaped by scarcity, not abundance

The traditional Ikarian diet resembles other Mediterranean eating patterns: beans and lentils, greens, vegetables, whole grains, olive oil, potatoes, herbs, fruit and modest amounts of fish. Meat and sweets historically appeared less often, in part because they were costly or reserved for celebrations.

Wild greens—some rich in antioxidants and micronutrients—are common. Herbal teas made from plants such as sage, rosemary or mountain herbs are also part of island life. Wine is usually consumed in small quantities and with food, though alcohol is not risk-free and should not be treated as a longevity prescription.

The broader pattern matters more than any ingredient. Ikarians traditionally eat minimally processed foods and relatively little added sugar. Americans, meanwhile, obtain a substantial share of their calories from ultra-processed products that are engineered for convenience and heavy consumption. Such diets are associated with obesity, diabetes and cardiovascular disease, all major threats to U.S. life expectancy.

## Meals are social events

On Ikaria, food is rarely only fuel. Meals can stretch for hours, and village festivals bring several generations together late into the night. Neighbors stop by without appointments. Older people remain visible and useful—as gardeners, cooks, caregivers, storytellers and keepers of local knowledge.

That social integration may be one of the island’s strongest advantages. Research in many countries links loneliness and social isolation with higher risks of depression, cognitive decline, heart disease and premature death.

The United States has material wealth and advanced medicine, but many Americans reach old age separated from extended family or disconnected from their communities. Suburban design, frequent relocation and demanding work schedules can make spontaneous contact difficult. Ikaria’s social life acts as an informal safety net: people notice when a neighbor is ill, absent or in need.

## Time works differently

Ikarians have a reputation for treating the clock as a suggestion. Shops may open late. Gatherings begin when people arrive. Afternoon naps are common, particularly in older generations.

This relaxed approach can frustrate visitors, but it may reduce chronic stress. Persistent stress raises levels of hormones that, over time, can contribute to high blood pressure, inflammation and metabolic disease. Adequate sleep also supports immune, cardiovascular and cognitive health.

The contrast with the United States is stark. Many Americans report short sleep, long commutes, job insecurity and little control over their schedules. Even leisure can become another task to optimize.

Still, Ikaria should not be romanticized. Island residents face economic strain, limited access to specialized health care and the same pressures of modernization found elsewhere. Younger generations eat more packaged food, drive more and move less than their grandparents did.

## Genes—and some uncertainty

Genetics may contribute to Ikarian longevity, but researchers generally view heredity as only part of the explanation. Family traits interact with diet, physical activity, social ties and environmental exposures.

There are also reasons to be cautious about dramatic claims. “Blue Zone” statistics depend on accurate birth and death records, and comparisons can be complicated by migration and small populations. Ikaria is not a controlled laboratory, and its customs cannot be separated neatly to show which one adds years to life.

Nor do all Ikarians live past 90. Some smoke, develop cancer or heart disease, and die young. The island offers population-level clues, not guarantees.

America’s lower life expectancy also reflects problems that go well beyond personal habits: unequal access to health care, poverty, gun violence, drug overdoses, dangerous roads and large disparities between racial and economic groups. An individual cannot solve those structural risks by eating beans or taking a nap.

## A life with purpose

Perhaps Ikaria’s most important lesson is that longevity is not pursued as a separate project. Older islanders often continue doing what they have always done—walking, gardening, cooking, visiting friends and helping family. Those activities supply movement, nutritious food, companionship and purpose at the same time.

Karimalis’s survival after a terminal diagnosis cannot prove why Ikarians live so long. But his return to the island captures the larger pattern. He did not retreat into a regimen built around extending life. He re-entered a community in which daily living itself supplied many of the conditions associated with healthy aging.

For Americans, the lesson is less about copying an exotic island than rebuilding what modern life has stripped away: regular movement, mostly unprocessed food, sufficient rest, dependable relationships and a reason to get up each morning.

Ikaria’s secret, if it has one, may be that these things are not treated as medicine. They are simply life.

## AC360° Guest Column  
### What Ikaria May Teach Us About Living Longer—and Better  
*By [Guest Author]*

On the Greek island of Ikaria, growing older does not always mean withdrawing from life. Residents often remain active well into their later years—tending gardens, walking steep roads, visiting neighbors and sharing meals that can stretch into the evening.

That reputation has brought longevity researcher and National Geographic explorer Dan Buettner to Ikaria as part of research associated with National Geographic and AARP. His goal is not to discover a single anti-aging ingredient, but to examine how diet, movement, social ties and the rhythms of daily life may work together over decades.

Ikaria has been identified as one of the world’s so-called “Blue Zones,” communities reported to have unusually high concentrations of long-lived residents. Buettner’s work has highlighted research suggesting that Ikarians experience comparatively high rates of survival into advanced age and, in some studies, lower levels of certain chronic diseases or cognitive impairment.

Possible explanations begin at the table. Traditional Ikarian meals tend to resemble a Mediterranean diet: vegetables, beans, whole grains, potatoes, olive oil, herbs and fruit, with more limited amounts of meat and highly processed food. Residents may also drink herbal teas and modest amounts of wine. No individual food has been proved to account for the island’s longevity, but the overall dietary pattern is consistent with broader evidence linking plant-forward Mediterranean diets to improved cardiovascular and metabolic health.

Food is only part of the picture. Daily life can involve frequent, low-intensity physical activity rather than scheduled exercise. Hilly terrain encourages walking, while gardening and household work keep people moving. Strong family networks, regular social contact, afternoon rest, religious participation and a less rigid sense of time may also help reduce isolation and chronic stress. Some Ikarians traditionally observe religious fasting periods, which may further reduce consumption of meat and calories at intervals.

These factors are plausible, but they should not be mistaken for proof. Most Blue Zones evidence is observational, making it difficult to separate culture and behavior from genetics, income, migration, health-care access or record-keeping. Researchers have also debated the accuracy of exceptional-age claims in some longevity regions. And modern Ikaria, like the rest of the world, is changing as younger residents adopt more sedentary routines and processed foods.

That is why the trip matters. The most useful lesson may not be a prescription to copy one island’s menu. It may be a broader question: What would our communities look like if healthy food, ordinary movement, social connection and a sense of purpose were built into everyday life rather than treated as individual acts of willpower?

Ikaria cannot offer immortality. It may, however, offer researchers a living case study in how environment and culture can make healthier choices feel natural—and how a longer life might also remain a connected and meaningful one.

**Editor’s note:** This is a guest commentary and does not represent the views of AC360° or its editorial staff. Dan Buettner’s “Blue Zones” framework has been developed through reporting and research collaborations, including work associated with National Geographic and AARP, and is also connected to commercial books and organizations. Claims about Ikarian longevity and its causes remain subjects of scientific study and debate. Observational findings do not establish that any particular food, habit or community practice causes longer life.

# Ikaria: Inside a Mediterranean Longevity Hotspot

In the eastern Aegean Sea, roughly 30 miles off the coast of Turkey, the Greek island of Ikaria has attracted international attention for the apparent health and longevity of its residents. Named after Icarus of Greek mythology, the mountainous island is frequently described as a “Blue Zone”—a place where people are reported to live unusually long lives while retaining comparatively good health.

Ikaria’s reputation is not based on a single miracle food or rigid wellness program. Instead, its longevity culture appears to emerge from a combination of traditional Mediterranean eating, regular low-intensity movement, strong social connections, restorative sleep, low time pressure, and a sense of optimism and belonging.

Although popular accounts sometimes exaggerate the island’s statistics, population studies do suggest that many older Ikarians have relatively favorable cardiovascular and metabolic health. Their way of life offers useful lessons, even if it cannot guarantee a particular lifespan.

## Healthy Aging on Ikaria

Ikaria became a focus of longevity research after demographic surveys identified a notable concentration of very old residents. The island has often been said to have an unusually high proportion of people reaching their 90s—sometimes described as several times the rate seen in countries such as the United States.

Research involving elderly Ikarians has reported relatively low rates of cardiovascular risk factors in some groups, along with substantial physical activity and continued social participation. Studies have also examined the island’s apparent levels of diabetes, depression, cognitive decline, and heart disease.

These findings require context. Longevity statistics can be difficult to verify because of migration, small populations, incomplete historical records, and differences in study methods. Ikaria is not free of chronic disease, and not every resident follows the traditional lifestyle. Genetics may play a role, while younger generations increasingly encounter processed foods, sedentary habits, and other modern health risks.

Even so, the island remains a compelling example of **healthspan**: not simply surviving into old age, but remaining engaged, mobile, and socially connected for much of life.

## A Traditional Mediterranean Diet

The Ikarian diet is a local version of the Mediterranean dietary pattern, built largely around minimally processed plant foods. Traditional meals commonly include:

- Wild greens and other vegetables  
- Beans, lentils, chickpeas, and black-eyed peas  
- Potatoes and whole grains  
- Olive oil  
- Fruit and nuts  
- Herbs, garlic, and onions  
- Modest amounts of fish  
- Goat or sheep dairy products  
- Smaller or less frequent portions of meat  
- Occasional wine, generally consumed with food and company  

Legumes are particularly important. They provide fiber, plant protein, potassium, magnesium, and slowly digested carbohydrates. Vegetables and wild greens contribute vitamins and polyphenols, while extra-virgin olive oil supplies primarily monounsaturated fat and antioxidant compounds.

This pattern may benefit health in several ways. High fiber intake supports digestive health and helps regulate blood sugar and cholesterol. Plant-rich meals tend to be less energy-dense than diets centered on processed foods and large portions of meat. Olive oil, nuts, vegetables, and legumes are also associated with cardiovascular benefits when consumed as part of a balanced Mediterranean diet.

Traditional Ikarian eating is not necessarily vegetarian. Rather, plant foods occupy the center of the plate, while animal foods tend to play a supporting role. Meals are often seasonal, locally sourced, and shared slowly with family or neighbors.

## Wild Greens and Everyday Foraging

Ikaria’s rugged landscape supports a wide range of edible wild plants. Residents have traditionally gathered greens such as dandelion, chicory, fennel, and other local varieties, depending on the season.

These plants are generally rich in fiber and micronutrients, and many contain diverse phytochemicals. Boiled greens may be served with olive oil and lemon, added to pies, or incorporated into stews. Foraging also adds a form of gentle physical activity: walking over uneven terrain, bending, carrying, and spending time outdoors.

The health value is therefore broader than the nutritional content of the greens themselves. It combines food knowledge, movement, contact with nature, and cultural continuity.

## Herbal Teas as a Daily Ritual

Herbal infusions are a familiar part of Ikarian life. Depending on availability and family tradition, residents may drink teas made from sage, rosemary, mint, oregano, mountain tea, or other local plants.

Many Mediterranean herbs contain polyphenols and aromatic compounds with antioxidant or anti-inflammatory activity in laboratory studies. Some herbs may also have mild diuretic, digestive, or relaxing effects. However, evidence that any individual tea directly extends human life is limited. The benefits are more plausibly understood as part of a larger pattern.

Herbal tea can replace heavily sweetened beverages, contribute to hydration, and create a natural pause in the day. Preparing and sharing tea also reinforces social bonds and routine—factors that matter for psychological as well as physical health.

“Natural” does not automatically mean risk-free. Concentrated herbal preparations can interact with medicines or be unsuitable during pregnancy or for certain medical conditions. The casual culinary use of herbs is different from taking high-dose extracts as supplements.

## Ikarian Honey

Honey occupies an important place in the island’s culinary traditions. Ikarian bees gather nectar from thyme, pine, heather, and other plants growing across the island’s largely uncultivated terrain. The resulting honey is valued for its distinctive flavor and is commonly added to tea, yogurt, bread, or desserts.

Honey contains small quantities of plant-derived compounds and has recognized antimicrobial properties in certain contexts. Darker or strongly flavored varieties may contain more phenolic compounds than highly processed sweeteners.

Still, honey is primarily a source of sugar. It should not be treated as a medicinal shortcut or consumed without restraint. Its place in the traditional Ikarian diet is generally modest: a flavorful sweetener within an otherwise nutrient-dense eating pattern, rather than a health food eaten in unlimited quantities.

## Mineral-Rich Hot Springs

Ikaria has long been known for thermal springs, particularly around the towns of Therma and Agios Kirykos. Some springs have been used since antiquity and contain minerals associated with geothermal activity.

Bathing in warm mineral water may promote relaxation, temporarily ease muscle or joint discomfort, and encourage social interaction. Heat can increase local blood flow and reduce the sensation of stiffness. For older adults, the psychological benefits of a calming ritual may be as meaningful as any mineral-specific effect.

Claims that hot springs cure chronic disease or directly increase longevity are not well established. Certain Ikarian springs also have naturally occurring radioactivity, so bathing should follow local safety guidance and medical advice, especially for people with cardiovascular conditions, pregnancy, or other health concerns.

## Low Stress and a Different Relationship With Time

One of Ikaria’s most frequently noted characteristics is its relaxed approach to schedules. Social events may begin late, shops may keep flexible hours, and daily routines often follow practical or communal needs rather than the clock.

This does not mean residents experience no hardship. Ikaria has a history marked by poverty, war, political exile, and geographic isolation. Yet traditional island life may reduce some forms of chronic stress through close community networks, shared resources, outdoor activity, and less emphasis on constant productivity.

Chronic psychological stress is associated with elevated blood pressure, sleep disruption, inflammation, and unhealthy coping behaviors. A culture that normalizes rest, companionship, and flexible time may buffer these effects.

Importantly, low stress in Ikaria is not merely the absence of work. Many older residents remain active in gardening, cooking, caring for relatives, tending animals, or participating in community life. Their days may be physically busy but psychologically less rushed.

## Sleep, Naps, and Late-Night Social Life

Sleep habits on Ikaria do not always resemble conventional advice built around an early, uninterrupted nighttime schedule. Residents may stay up late for festivals, meals, or visits, then sleep later or take afternoon naps.

Napping is common in many Mediterranean cultures, especially during hot weather. Short daytime naps may improve alertness and reduce fatigue. Some observational research has associated occasional napping with cardiovascular benefits, although results vary and can be complicated by underlying illness, nap duration, and poor nighttime sleep.

The broader lesson is not that everyone should stay awake late or take long daily naps. Rather, Ikarian routines often allow sleep to respond to social rhythms, temperature, and individual fatigue. Rest is treated as a normal part of life rather than a sign of laziness.

For most adults, adequate sleep duration and regularity remain important. Persistent daytime sleepiness or unusually long naps may indicate sleep apnea, depression, medication effects, or other medical concerns.

## Optimism, Purpose, and Social Connection

Older Ikarians often remain embedded in family and community life. They attend religious celebrations, visit neighbors, work in gardens, prepare food, play games, dance, and participate in festivals. These activities offer both companionship and a reason to keep moving.

Optimism in this context does not necessarily mean constant cheerfulness. It may be better understood as resilience: confidence that difficulties can be endured, help will be available, and tomorrow will still contain meaningful tasks.

Social connection is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of health. Isolation and loneliness are associated with higher risks of depression, cognitive decline, cardiovascular disease, and premature death. Ikaria’s dense social fabric may help protect residents by providing:

- Emotional support  
- Practical help during illness  
- Regular cognitive stimulation  
- A sense of identity and belonging  
- Informal monitoring by relatives and neighbors  
- Frequent reasons to leave the house and remain active  

Festivals, in particular, combine several potentially beneficial behaviors: walking, dancing, eating, conversation, music, and intergenerational contact.

## Movement Without Formal Exercise

Traditional Ikarian life naturally includes low- to moderate-intensity physical activity. The island’s steep roads and footpaths make walking physically demanding. Gardening, farming, kneading bread, gathering herbs, chopping wood, and maintaining a home also require frequent movement.

This differs from exercising for a fixed period and then remaining sedentary for the rest of the day. Ikarians historically accumulated activity in small amounts over many hours, often with a practical purpose.

Such movement helps preserve leg strength, balance, cardiovascular fitness, and metabolic health. Weight-bearing activity is also important for bone health, while gardening and household tasks can support dexterity and independence.

## Wine, Moderation, and Context

Wine is part of traditional Ikarian food culture and is often consumed in small quantities with meals or at social gatherings. Local red wine contains polyphenols, but alcohol itself carries real health risks. Even moderate consumption may raise the risk of certain cancers, and higher intake increases the risk of liver disease, hypertension, accidents, and dependence.

For that reason, wine should not be considered necessary for longevity. People who do not drink should not begin for health reasons. Any apparent benefit in Mediterranean populations may partly reflect the context in which wine is consumed: small amounts, food, slow meals, friendship, and an otherwise healthy lifestyle.

## Why the Whole Lifestyle Matters

Attempts to reduce Ikarian longevity to honey, mountain tea, wine, or a particular herb miss the central point. The island’s traditional lifestyle works as a system:

- Plant-centered meals support cardiovascular and metabolic health.  
- Everyday movement maintains strength and mobility.  
- Rest and naps help counter fatigue.  
- Social networks reduce isolation and provide practical support.  
- Gardening and household work create purpose.  
- Outdoor life brings sunlight, nature, and regular activity.  
- Flexible schedules may reduce chronic time pressure.  
- Optimism and cultural continuity promote resilience.  

These factors reinforce one another. A person who gardens gains vegetables, physical activity, sunlight, purpose, and opportunities to share food. Someone who walks to visit a neighbor receives exercise and social contact at the same time. A communal meal may provide nutritious food, emotional support, and slower eating.

## Lessons Beyond the Island

It is neither possible nor necessary to replicate Ikarian life exactly. The island’s customs grew from its geography, history, economy, and culture. Still, several practical principles can be adapted elsewhere:

1. **Make plants the foundation of most meals.** Eat more beans, vegetables, whole grains, nuts, herbs, and olive oil.
2. **Move throughout the day.** Walk, garden, use stairs, cook, and perform active household tasks.
3. **Protect sleep and allow genuine rest.** Aim for adequate nighttime sleep and use naps thoughtfully.
4. **Build recurring social rituals.** Shared meals, clubs, volunteering, worship, and neighborhood gatherings create reliable connection.
5. **Maintain a sense of purpose.** Continue learning, helping, creating, and contributing at every age.
6. **Use traditional foods realistically.** Herbal tea and honey can be enjoyable, but neither is a cure-all.
7. **Reduce avoidable time pressure.** Create periods in which meals, conversations, and rest are not rushed.
8. **Avoid romanticizing alcohol.** Social connection and a Mediterranean meal do not require wine.
9. **Cultivate realistic optimism.** Resilience grows through relationships, meaningful activity, and confidence in one’s ability to cope.

## A Model of Longevity as Culture

Ikaria’s significance lies less in a secret ingredient than in its picture of aging as an active, social, and meaningful stage of life. Traditional residents do not necessarily “pursue wellness” as a separate project. Health-supporting behaviors are woven into eating, working, resting, visiting, and celebrating.

Scientific uncertainties remain, and the island should not be portrayed as a disease-free paradise. Yet Ikaria offers a persuasive idea: long life is shaped not only by medical care or individual discipline, but also by the environments and cultures that make healthy choices ordinary.

Its enduring lesson is that healthy aging may be nurtured through simple foods, regular movement, sufficient rest, enduring relationships, and the expectation that life can remain purposeful well into old age.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a first-person CNN opinion piece titled around the secret to living longer, contrasting American life expectancy and chronic disease with the unusually healthy nonagenarians of Ikaria, Greece.
counterfactuals.output:
# The secret to living longer may be living for more than yourself

**Opinion**

When I first arrived on Ikaria, a rugged Greek island in the eastern Aegean, I expected to hear about a miraculous diet or some obscure herb that kept residents alive into their 90s.

Instead, I found older people tending gardens, walking steep roads, lingering over meals and making plans for the next village festival. Many remained deeply involved in the lives of their families and neighbors. They were not pursuing longevity as a personal optimization project. They were simply living in a culture that made healthy choices feel ordinary.

That distinction matters.

In the United States, life expectancy was about 78.4 years in 2023, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Chronic illnesses such as heart disease, cancer and diabetes remain leading causes of death and disability. Millions of Americans spend their later years managing multiple conditions, taking an array of medications and navigating a health care system that often intervenes only after disease has taken hold.

Ikaria offers a striking contrast. The island is frequently identified as a longevity hot spot, with an unusually high share of residents living into their 90s and historically low reported rates of some age-related diseases. No single habit explains that pattern, and we should be skeptical of romantic claims that any community has “solved” aging. Genetics, migration, record-keeping and access to medical diagnosis can all shape longevity statistics.

Still, the texture of daily life on Ikaria suggests lessons that American medicine too often neglects.

Ikarians traditionally eat a version of the Mediterranean diet: vegetables, beans, whole grains, olive oil and modest amounts of meat and processed food. They move throughout the day, not necessarily by going to a gym but by walking, gardening, cooking and visiting friends. Their routines create natural opportunities for activity.

But the most powerful ingredient may be harder to package and sell: belonging.

On Ikaria, social connection is not treated as an optional luxury. Long meals, religious celebrations, family obligations and village festivals knit people together. Older adults are not automatically pushed to the margins. They continue to contribute, advise, work and participate.

In America, by contrast, we often make health an individual assignment. We tell people to exercise more, eat better, sleep eight hours and reduce stress — as though those goals exist apart from working hours, wages, housing, neighborhood safety and social isolation.

Then we build communities that make those instructions difficult to follow.

Many Americans must drive to reach a grocery store, a friend’s home or even a safe place to walk. Work schedules can leave little time for cooking or rest. Older adults may retire not only from their jobs but also from a central source of identity and social contact. Loneliness has become so widespread that the US surgeon general has described it as a serious public health concern.

We cannot supplement our way out of that problem.

This is where the mythology surrounding places such as Ikaria can become misleading. The lesson is not that Americans should drink a particular tea, copy a Greek recipe or take an afternoon nap and expect to reach 100. The lesson is that longevity emerges from an ecosystem.

Diet matters. Movement matters. Sleep matters. Medical care matters. But so do purpose, trust and the expectation that someone will notice if you fail to show up.

I have come to believe that the American conversation about aging is too focused on extending lifespan and not focused enough on building a life people can remain connected to. We celebrate independence, but longevity often depends on interdependence — on relatives, neighbors and institutions that make it possible to stay useful and engaged.

That does not mean importing island life wholesale. Ikaria has its own hardships, and its traditions developed under conditions very different from those in the United States. Nor should we blame individuals who become sick in environments that promote sedentary behavior, stress and cheap ultra-processed food.

But we can design better environments.

Cities can create walkable neighborhoods and accessible public spaces. Employers can offer schedules that leave room for sleep, meals and relationships. Communities can support multigenerational housing, local gathering places and programs that treat older adults as participants rather than patients. Health care systems can ask about loneliness and purpose alongside blood pressure and cholesterol.

And each of us can reconsider what a healthy life looks like. It may involve more beans and fewer packaged foods. It may mean walking to see a friend instead of tracking another solitary workout. It may mean protecting time for shared meals, volunteering or checking on an older neighbor.

Ikaria’s nonagenarians do not possess a secret that can be bottled. Their message is both simpler and more demanding: A long life is shaped not only by what we consume, but also by how we move through the world and whom we move through it with.

If America wants to live longer, we should stop searching only for a cure for aging. We should start building a society in which people have reasons — and companions — to keep living.
